entry.title: What Moving Between Industry and Academia Made Me Unlearn

link.title: What Moving Between Industry and Academia Made Me Unlearn

entry.content:
I have spent the last several years moving between two worlds that each like to explain the other one to themselves. I built warehouse robots in Tokyo, left for Seoul to do a PhD in legged robots, and came back to Ho Chi Minh City to work on manipulation. When people ask about those moves, they usually ask about the hardware, as if the interesting part were the actuators. It was not. The interesting part was what each move forced me to unlearn.

The last mile is the product

Tokyo was my first real job in industry, and it taught me a lesson I was not ready for. A robot that works in the lab and dies on a customer’s floor is not ninety percent done. It is zero percent done.

In the lab, the environment cooperates. The floor is level, the lighting is the lighting you set, and the person operating the machine is the same person who wrote the code. On a customer’s site, none of that holds. The floor has a slope nobody mentioned in the spec. The operator does something you never simulated, because it was the obvious thing to do and no one thought it needed simulating. The robot that looked finished in the demo video spends its first week on site discovering an entire category of failure that did not exist in your test suite.

I had been taught to think of deployment as the final step in a long sequence, the thing you get to once everything else is done. Tokyo taught me it is the product. The integration, the failure modes, the operator who finds the gap in your assumptions and does not care that the assumption was reasonable — that is the thing you are actually selling. The robot is just the part you could already build in the lab. What separates a company from a lab is everything that happens after the lab stops being involved.

A data problem wearing a robot costume

Seoul was the opposite direction: out of industry and into research, for a PhD on how legged machines walk. I went in expecting a controls problem. I came out convinced it was mostly something else.

For years the field had treated locomotion as a matter of better models and tighter controllers, and there was real, hard-won progress in that direction. But the honest conclusion, after spending that time inside it, was that we did not yet have the compute or the data to make general locomotion cheap. What looked like a robotics problem was, underneath, a data problem wearing a robot costume.

That is a harder thing to unlearn than it sounds, because it changes what the word progress means. If the bottleneck is data, then a demo that works on one robot, in one lab, under one carefully held set of conditions is not a preview of the future. It is a sample of one. And a sample of one does not generalize, no matter how cleanly the video cuts. The habit I had to break was treating an impressive single result as evidence about a general capability, when the actual constraint was sitting one layer below the thing everyone was celebrating.

The unlearning is the skill

Looking back, the through-line between Tokyo and Seoul was not any piece of hardware. It was the same realization arriving from two directions: some problems you cannot skip.

Tokyo said you cannot skip the last mile, no matter how much of the rest you have already finished. Seoul said you cannot skip the data, no matter how elegant the model sitting on top of it. Both are versions of the same mistake, which is mistaking the part you enjoy for the part that matters.

This is, I think, the most underrated skill a person can build across a career that crosses industry and research: the ability to notice which problems are being skipped, and to say so before the schedule runs out. It is not a technical skill, and it cannot be taught in a lecture. It is only acquired by being in the room when the skip happens and watching what it costs. Both transitions cost me a version of that lesson, and it was worth more than everything technical I picked up along the way.

Coming back, and staying honest

Now I am back in industry, working on manipulation, and I teach Smart Vehicle OS at NTT University on the side. The teaching is not a side project in the way people assume. It is the thing that keeps me honest.

A classroom does not let you get away with the kind of confidence a demo video does. Students ask the question you were hoping nobody would ask, because they do not yet know which assumptions are supposed to be sacred. They will find the one you buried, and they will do it in front of the rest of the class. Every term I have to say out loud what is actually generalizable and what is just a demo that got lucky. Saying it out loud is how I check that I actually believe it, and it is the reason I have not stopped teaching even when the work gets busy.

The question that follows me into the work now is no longer can we build it. It is can we train it, and will it survive contact. That shift in the question is the real product of the last few years. The hardware was never the hard part; it was always the part you could point at.

A question instead of a conclusion

If you have moved between research and industry, I would like to know the one thing the transition forced you to unlearn. Not the thing you learned — those are easy to list on a resume. The thing you had to let go of: the belief that turned out to be wrong, the confidence that turned out to be unearned.

I suspect those unlearned things are where the actual expertise lives, and that we talk about them far less than we should. We report the skills and stay quiet about the beliefs that had to die to make room for them, which is a strange way to describe a career, and probably the wrong one.
entry.summary: The career moves that mattered most were the lessons I had to unlearn, not the skills I picked up.

entry.title: A Working Demo Is Not a Working System

link.title: A Working Demo Is Not a Working System

entry.content:
I teach Smart Vehicle OS at NTT University, and the hardest part of the course is not the syllabus. It is convincing students that a working demo and a working system are two different species.

By mid-semester most of them can train a model, run a motion planner in simulation, and show a clean trajectory on a clean map. The demo works. Then the code meets the vehicle, and the vehicle does not care about the demo.

A sensor drops out for 200 ms. A timestamp drifts. An edge case nobody labelled appears in the middle of the frame. The planner that looked correct on a laptop now steers into a wall while the logs insist everything is fine. Nothing in the previous twelve weeks prepares a student for that moment, because nothing in the previous twelve weeks was allowed to fail.

The gap is not knowledge, it is diagnosis

The students who struggle are rarely the ones who do not understand the theory. They understand it better than I did at their age. What they lack is the habit of asking which assumption just broke, and the tools to answer it.

A demo is built on assumptions that are never written down: the clock is shared, the bus is not saturated, the sensor is calibrated, the map is current, the compute is not thermally throttled. A system is what remains when you remove those assumptions one at a time and the behaviour stays within bounds.

That distinction is easy to state and hard to teach, because the failure modes live in the seams between subsystems. A timestamp drift is not a perception bug or a control bug. It is a systems bug that presents as both.

Teaching it backwards

This year I rebuilt the course around failure. Every module opens with a real malfunction taken from a deployed system, and the students work backwards to a root cause before they are allowed to build anything.

The malfunctions are deliberately unglamorous:

  • Two nodes disagree about time by 40 ms, and the fusion output starts oscillating while every individual component reports healthy.
  • A CAN bus saturates under logging load, frames drop silently, and the controller sees stale commands rather than errors.
  • A motor controller heats up over a long run, its torque constant shifts, and a controller tuned in the first ten minutes starts overshooting in the fortieth.
  • A camera pipeline drops frames under CPU contention, and the perception stack interpolates across the gap as if nothing happened.

None of these would appear in an architecture diagram. All of them would end a deployment.

Working backwards from a failure changes what students pay attention to. They stop asking “does my module work?” and start asking “what does my module assume about the modules around it?” That is the question that separates an engineer who can integrate a system from one who can only assemble it.

The uncomfortable part

This approach is slower. You cover less material. A student who spends a week chasing a clock skew does not spend that week learning a new planner. On a syllabus measured in topics covered, failure-first teaching looks like a regression.

I think that measurement is wrong, and the industry feedback agrees with me. The expensive mistakes in robotics are not algorithm choices. They are integration failures discovered late, when the schedule has no room left to discover anything.

What cannot be imported

There is a broader argument here about where robotics capability actually comes from.

Vietnam’s robotics sector is growing, and most of the core stack is still imported: reducers, controllers, sensors, drive electronics. That is a normal stage of development, and importing hardware is not the problem. Hardware can be ordered, and it arrives with a datasheet.

What cannot be ordered is a generation of engineers who can take that hardware, integrate it into a system, and diagnose it when the system misbehaves in a way no datasheet predicted. Countries that built durable robotics industries did it on unglamorous systems courses, long before their robots looked impressive in public.

If our programmes stop at demos, we will keep importing the part that matters most: the people who can close the gap between a component that works on a bench and a machine that works in the world.

A question for the people on the other side

If you teach engineering in Vietnam, I would like to know the one thing you wish industry understood about your students.

And if you hire robotics engineers, I would like to know the opposite: what is the first thing a new graduate gets wrong on a real system, the thing no transcript predicted?

I suspect the answers overlap more than either side expects.

Smart Vehicle OS is taught at NTT University. The failure catalogue above is drawn from deployed systems; the course structure is an ongoing experiment and I will write about what worked and what did not at the end of the semester.
entry.summary: Why a robotics course should start from failure, not from architecture diagrams.

entry.title: Run Huggingface Models Locally For Free

link.title: Run Huggingface Models Locally For Free

entry.content:
If you’ve been following AI advancements in the open-source space, you’ve likely heard of Hugging Face. This French-American company is dedicated to open-source machine learning tools, particularly focusing on natural language processing. Hugging Face is named after a cute emoji.

Hugging Face’s Core Offerings

Hugging Face provides several key tools to empower developers and researchers in the AI community:

  • Transformers Library: This is a collection of pre-trained models designed for various tasks such as text classification, translation, summarization, and more.
  • Datasets Library: A repository offering ready-to-use datasets for training and evaluating machine learning models.
  • Hugging Face Hub: A central platform that functions like the GitHub of AI, allowing users to share and explore models, datasets, and machine learning applications. It facilitates collaboration among machine learning enthusiasts and experts, enabling them to learn from each other’s work and experience.

Understanding Key Hugging Face Terminologies

To maximize your experience with Hugging Face, it’s helpful to understand some core terms:

Pre-trained Model

A pre-trained model is a machine learning model that has already been taught using a large amount of data for a specific task, such as recognizing images or understanding language. This means you can use it immediately without needing to train it from scratch.

Inference

Inference is the process where a trained model makes predictions or draws conclusions about new, previously unseen data, based on patterns it learned during its training phase.

Training

Training is the initial phase of the machine learning process where the machine learns by being exposed to numerous examples. For instance, if you’re teaching it to recognize cars, you provide it with many labeled pictures of different cars, allowing the machine to build its understanding. Once trained, the machine uses this acquired knowledge during inference to recognize new things, like a car it hasn’t seen before.

Transformers

Transformers are a type of model specifically designed to handle text-based tasks, including translation, summarization, and text generation. Their unique architecture uses “attention mechanisms” to identify and capture the relationships between words and sentences.

Tokenizer

A tokenizer is a process that breaks down text into smaller units known as tokens. These tokens are typically words or subwords and are essential for natural language processing tasks.

Getting Started with Hugging Face

To begin using Hugging Face, you’ll need to set up an account and install the necessary libraries and dependencies.

Account Setup

Signing up as a community individual contributor is free. You can create a free account by visiting the Hugging Face website and clicking “sign up”. You may need to complete a quick human verification, then enter your email and password, complete your profile, and generate an avatar. After creating the account, you’ll receive a verification link in your email that you must click to verify your address. Once verified, you are officially a Hugging Face member. For more features or organizational needs, pro or customized plans are available.

Environment Setup: Python, Pip, and Virtual Environments

Before using the Hugging Face Hub programmatically, you must set up your environment:

  1. Install Python and Pip: Ensure Python 3.8 or higher is installed. Pip, Python’s package manager, is included with Python and doesn’t need separate installation.
  2. Create a Virtual Environment: It’s recommended to create a virtual environment to isolate project dependencies from system-wide packages, leading to a cleaner and more manageable setup. Common options include Venv (included with Python 3.3+) and Conda (installed via Anaconda or Miniconda), which is popular for data science and ML projects. You can activate your environment using the conda activate command.
  3. Choose a Code Editor/IDE: For development, you can use any preferred code editor or IDE, such as Jupyter Notebook, PyCharm, or Visual Studio Code.

Installing Hugging Face Libraries

Hugging Face offers two main libraries for accessing pre-trained models:

  • Transformers: This library handles text-based tasks like translation, summarization, and text generation. Install it using pip install transformers.
  • Diffusers: This library manages image-based tasks, including image synthesis, image editing, and image captioning.

To enable the pipeline function (discussed next) to load models, you’ll also need a model backend like PyTorch or TensorFlow. To install TensorFlow, run pip install TensorFlow.

Using Pre-trained Models with Hugging Face

The Pipeline Function

The pipeline function, imported from the Hugging Face Transformers library, is a high-level helper function that simplifies the use of pre-trained models for common tasks. It automates processes like loading the appropriate model, tokenizing input, running the model, and formatting output, requiring only a few lines of code.

Example: Sentiment Analysis with DistilBERT

Here’s how you can use the pipeline function for sentiment analysis:

  1. Import the pipeline: from transformers import pipeline.

  2. Load the pre-trained model: Use pipeline with the sentiment-analysis parameter and specify a model like "distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst2-english".

    • DistilBERT is a smaller, faster version of the BERT model.
    • base uncased means it processes lowercase text and disregards capitalization.
    • fine-tuned on SST2 indicates it was specifically trained for sentiment classification using the SST2 dataset.

    This setup creates a ready-to-use tool to determine if a sentence’s sentiment is positive or negative.

  3. Analyze text: Store your desired text in a variable (e.g., inputtext), then call the pipeline with this variable and print the output.
  4. Run the code: Ensure the correct Conda environment is active. If using VS Code, select the appropriate Python interpreter via the command palette (Shift+Command+P). Execute the Python file from the terminal (e.g., python your_file_name.py).

The model will return the sentiment analysis. For example, it identified one text as negative with 99.96% confidence and another positive sentence confidently as positive. The process demonstrates how straightforward it is to get a pre-trained model running using Hugging Face libraries. A dependency conflict (Keras) was resolved by installing the recommended version during one execution.

Discovering and Exploring Models

Finding the right pre-trained model for a specific task is simple on the Hugging Face website. You can browse models and filter them by task, library, language, and other criteria. Models and datasets can also be searched by keyword and sorted by trending, most likes, most downloads, or recent updates.

Every model on the Hugging Face Hub has a “model card” containing important information such as model details, usage examples, links to files, and community interaction features. You can also view “Spaces” that use a particular model and explore them further or even clone a Space to your local machine to run it yourself.
entry.summary: a step-to-step guideline to run huggingface models locally
